facts.title: A Name Meaning Heavy Stone
facts.text: The English name tungsten comes from the Swedish words 'tung sten,' literally 'heavy stone,' a nod to the dense mineral scheelite from which it was first recognized. Confusingly, its chemical symbol is W, from 'wolfram,' the name still used in German and many other languages and derived from the ore wolframite. The element is the only one whose common English name and chemical symbol come from completely different words and languages.

facts.title: Two Brothers and a Bishop
facts.text: In 1781 the Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele showed that the mineral scheelite contained a new acid, but he did not isolate the metal itself. The credit for first isolating tungsten in 1783 goes to the Spanish brothers Juan José and Fausto Elhuyar, who reduced tungstic oxide with charcoal at the Royal Seminary of Bergara. Their careful work turned Scheele's chemical hint into a real, weighable metal.

facts.title: Champion of Melting Points
facts.text: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal and of any element except carbon, melting at a blistering 3,422 degrees Celsius (6,192 degrees Fahrenheit). It also boils at around 5,930 degrees Celsius, one of the highest boiling points known. This extreme heat resistance is why tungsten survives conditions that would vaporize almost anything else.

facts.title: The Glow Inside Light Bulbs
facts.text: For most of the twentieth century, the thin glowing wire inside incandescent light bulbs was made of tungsten, a design perfected by William Coolidge at General Electric in 1909. Its sky-high melting point let the filament run white-hot, around 2,500 degrees Celsius, without melting or quickly evaporating. The same property makes tungsten ideal for the heating elements and electrodes in many high-temperature devices.

facts.title: As Dense as Gold
facts.text: Tungsten is remarkably heavy, with a density of about 19.3 grams per cubic centimeter, almost exactly the same as pure gold and nearly twice that of lead. Because of this, tungsten alloys are used for radiation shielding, fishing weights, dart barrels, and the balance weights in race cars and aircraft. Its density combined with low cost compared to gold even makes it a notorious material for faking gold bars.

facts.title: Harder Than Steel as Carbide
facts.text: When tungsten is combined with carbon to form tungsten carbide, the result is an extraordinarily hard ceramic-like material that approaches the hardness of diamond. Tungsten carbide tips and tools cut, drill, and machine metals that would dull ordinary steel almost instantly. It is also used for the rotating ball in many ballpoint pens and for hard-wearing jewelry rings.

facts.title: A Metal That Bacteria Crave
facts.text: Tungsten is the heaviest element known to be used by living things, appearing in enzymes of certain heat-loving microbes. Archaea such as Pyrococcus furiosus, which thrive near deep-sea hydrothermal vents, use tungsten-containing enzymes to power their metabolism at temperatures above 100 degrees Celsius. This makes tungsten a rare case of a 'heavy' metal playing an essential biological role rather than merely being toxic.

facts.title: Forged in Dying Stars
facts.text: Tungsten is a relatively rare element in the universe, formed mainly in the violent deaths of massive stars and in neutron-star mergers through rapid neutron capture. In Earth's crust it makes up only about 1.25 parts per million, and it is never found as a free metal in nature. Instead it occurs locked inside minerals such as wolframite and scheelite, with China today mining the majority of the world's supply.

facts.title: Five Naturally Occurring Isotopes
facts.text: Natural tungsten is a mix of five isotopes, with tungsten-184 and tungsten-186 being the most abundant. For decades all of them were thought to be perfectly stable, but extremely sensitive experiments later showed that tungsten-180 is faintly radioactive, decaying by alpha emission. Its half-life is about 1.8 quintillion years, vastly longer than the current age of the universe, so a sample of tungsten effectively lasts forever.

facts.title: Guardian Against Fusion Heat
facts.text: Inside experimental fusion reactors like ITER in southern France, tungsten is being used to line the divertor, the region that faces the hottest exhaust of the plasma. Engineers chose tungsten because its record melting point and low erosion let it endure heat loads comparable to the surface of the Sun. The same toughness has put tungsten into rocket nozzles, armor-piercing projectiles, and the electrodes used in arc welding.
